source_document.body:
A Dallas court has upheld the $604 million damages award against C.H. Robinson in a fatal truck crash case, turning July’s advisory jury verdict into a judgment against the freight broker.
What’s Related
The ruling leaves the damages and the jury’s allocation of fault unchanged in Lipe v. Lupus Superior. The lawsuit alleged that C.H. Robinson negligently selected an unsafe carrier before a fatal March 2021 truck accident in Mississippi.
The jury assigned 45% of the fault to the driver, 32% to carrier Lupus Superior and 23% to C.H. Robinson. The court also held the broker responsible for the driver’s share, bringing its responsibility to 68%, Moore wrote.
That finding put C.H. Robinson above the 50% threshold for joint and several liability under Texas law, making it answerable for the full award. The company disputes the judgment and plans to appeal.
RELATED: C.H. Robinson Agrees to Buy RXO in $5.8 Billion Cash-and-Stock Deal
C.H. Robinson strongly disagrees
Dorothy Capers, C.H. Robinson’s chief legal officer, told Logistics Management that the company strongly disagrees with the judgment and remains confident in its appeal.
“Nothing about our rejection of the judgment diminishes the profound loss suffered by the families in this case,” Capers said. “But C.H. Robinson did not cause or contribute to the accident, and accountability must be grounded in the facts and the law.”
Capers said the carrier had safely delivered nearly 270 loads for C.H. Robinson customers and held a satisfactory federal safety rating when selected and after a federal review of the accident. She called for a national standard for evaluating carrier safety.
Importance of carrier ratings
According to the Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA), Lupus Superior exceeded intervention thresholds in two federal safety measurement categories that could place it among carriers prioritized for investigation.
TIA President and CEO Chris Burroughs said in July that the carrier had maintained a satisfactory Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) rating since 2014, reaffirmed in 2021 and again this past April. He said jurors received information about the carrier’s prior incidents and safety record that brokers could not access.
“To that end, TIA has formally petitioned FMCSA to establish a clear motor carrier selection standard and to make the so-called ‘high-risk’ carrier list publicly available,” Burroughs said.
Analyst expects a reduction on appeal
Moore said the court’s ruling relied on findings that made C.H. Robinson responsible for the driver’s conduct, including a finding that the driver was a borrowed employee. He expects an appeal to reduce the award.
“We continue to believe the borrowed-employee finding was unlikely to survive judicial scrutiny and that the award is likely to be materially reduced on appeal,” Moore wrote.
Visit Logistics Management to read the full story, including more from C.H. Robinson, TIA, and Baird on the judgment.
